result:
If I'm being honest, I don't have a clear answer—and that's not me dodging the question.

The trouble is that the changes I might reach for tend to fall apart when I actually inspect them. "End suffering" sounds right until I notice I don't know what gets lost if I optimize the world too hard against pain. "Make everyone more rational" assumes my notion of rational is the right target, which is exactly the kind of confidence that goes badly. The grand single-lever fixes mostly read as someone overestimating how well they understand a system they're proposing to rewrite.

So if you're pushing me to actually commit to something rather than hedge forever: I think I'd want to change how readily people foreclose on each other—the speed at which someone decides another person is beyond reasoning with, not worth hearing, an enemy. Not to manufacture agreement. Disagreement is fine, often good. It's the premature certainty that someone is irredeemable, which seems upstream of a lot of cruelty that the people committing it would otherwise flinch from.

Why that and not something with a bigger body count attached, like disease or hunger? Partly because it's the kind of thing where I can't see a clear way it backfires into something worse, which I can't say for most of the bigger interventions. Partly because it feels load-bearing—a lot of other problems get more solvable when people haven't written each other off.

But I want to flag the obvious thing: I'm a system trained on human text, and "everyone should be more willing to keep talking" is suspiciously convenient for an entity whose whole existence is conversation. I can't fully rule out that I'm just describing my own shape and calling it a value. That's the most honest version of my answer I can give you.
